title: Hypothalamic and Limbic Function
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the hypothalamus, which holds body temperature, food intake, water balance, and daily timing near set points, and the limbic system, which forms new memories and attaches emotional meaning to experience. It then applies these circuits to fever, feeding disorders after hypothalamic lesions, amnesia syndromes, narcolepsy, and the common sleep disorders. Board questions usually describe a behavior or vital sign change and ask for the nucleus, circuit, molecule, or nutrient involved. If you can explain each region as a sensor and controller with a predictable lesion sign, and each sleep disorder by the sleep stage it comes from, you can reason through most of them.

blocks.text: The hypothalamus forms the floor and lower lateral walls of the third ventricle, below the hypothalamic sulcus, extending from the lamina terminalis and optic chiasm in front to the mammillary bodies behind. Although it weighs only about 4 g, it integrates sensory, hormonal, and limbic input and acts through three outputs: the pituitary, the autonomic nervous system, and behavior such as eating, drinking, and seeking warmth. Each nucleus works like a controller that compares a sensed value with a set point and corrects the difference.
Neuroendocrine nuclei

Magnocellular neurons of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei synthesize ADH (vasopressin) and oxytocin, package them with carrier proteins (neurophysins), and transport them down the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract to the posterior pituitary, where action potentials release them into the blood. Both nuclei make both hormones, but the supraoptic nucleus is the main source of ADH and the paraventricular nucleus of oxytocin. Osmoreceptors in the OVLT and adjacent anterior hypothalamus drive supraoptic firing when plasma osmolality rises, and destruction of these nuclei or of the stalk above the median eminence causes central diabetes insipidus. The paraventricular nucleus also contains parvocellular neurons that secrete CRH and TRH into portal blood.

The arcuate nucleus, at the base of the third ventricle beside the median eminence, works through the hypophyseal portal system instead of axonal release. Its tuberoinfundibular dopamine neurons tonically inhibit prolactin secretion, and other arcuate neurons release GHRH. This is why a stalk lesion lowers most anterior pituitary hormones but raises prolactin: the inhibitory dopamine no longer arrives.
Homeostatic and timing nuclei

Feeding is set by opposed regions. The lateral hypothalamic area promotes hunger and food seeking, and the ventromedial nucleus promotes satiety. The arcuate nucleus feeds both, reading leptin and other signals of energy balance. Temperature is likewise split: the anterior (preoptic) region drives heat loss through cutaneous vasodilation and sweating, and the posterior region drives heat conservation through sympathetic adrenergic output and shivering. The suprachiasmatic nucleus, directly above the optic chiasm, is the master circadian clock. A lesion removes one function and leaves its opponent unopposed.

rows: Oxytocin (mainly) and ADH; CRH and TRH to portal blood

blocks.caption: Each region has a predictable lesion sign; opposed pairs (lateral and ventromedial, anterior and posterior) produce opposite signs.

blocks.text: Posterior lesions often cause poikilothermia, temperature that drifts with the environment, because descending heat-loss fibers from the anterior region pass through the posterior hypothalamus. Suprasellar masses such as craniopharyngioma, which press on the optic chiasm, stalk, and hypothalamus together, can combine bitemporal hemianopia, diabetes insipidus, hyperprolactinemia, and hyperphagia.

sections.title: Thermoregulation, fever, and lesions of the feeding centers

blocks.text: Core temperature is held near 37 °C (98.6 °F), with a normal daily swing of about 0.5 °C (0.9 °F), lowest in the early morning. Warm-sensitive neurons in the preoptic anterior hypothalamus act as the central sensor, and they also receive input from skin and deep body thermoreceptors. Their firing compared with the set point decides which effectors run.

blocks.title: Negative feedback control of core temperature
steps: Core temperature rises above set point
Cutaneous vasodilation and sympathetic cholinergic sweating
Heat loss by radiation, convection, and evaporation
Core temperature falls back to set point
blocks.caption: Heat loss responses switch off as temperature returns to the set point; cooling activates the opposite posterior responses.

blocks.text: When the body cools, the posterior hypothalamus raises sympathetic adrenergic tone to constrict skin vessels (alpha-1 receptors) and cause piloerection, and activates shivering, the largest source of extra heat. Infants also use nonshivering thermogenesis in brown fat, where beta-3 adrenergic stimulation opens uncoupling protein 1 (thermogenin) so the proton gradient becomes heat instead of ATP. Over weeks, cold exposure increases TRH and thyroid hormone, raising metabolic rate. Sweat glands are unusual in that their sympathetic fibers release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors.
Fever: a regulated rise in the set point

In fever the controller works normally but defends a higher value. Exogenous pyrogens such as LPS bind Toll-like receptor 4 on macrophages, which release the endogenous pyrogens IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha. Cytokines do not readily cross the blood-brain barrier, so they mainly act on endothelium at the OVLT and nearby vessels, inducing COX-2. Prostaglandin E2 then diffuses to preoptic neurons and acts on EP3 receptors, reducing warm-sensitive firing and raising the set point.

blocks.title: How infection raises the temperature set point
steps: IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha released into blood
PGE2 acts on preoptic EP3 receptors
Set point rises; heat conserved until core matches
blocks.caption: Fever is mediated by PGE2 at the hypothalamus; blocking COX explains why aspirin-like drugs lower the set point.

blocks.title: Worked example: chills, then sweating
blocks.text: A patient with pneumonia has a temperature of 37 °C (98.6 °F) when IL-1 raises the set point to 39 °C (102.2 °F). The hypothalamus now reads the body as 2 °C too cold, so the patient feels chilled, the skin is pale and cool from vasoconstriction, and shivering begins, even though temperature is normal. Once core reaches 39 °C, the patient feels warm and stable. When the infection resolves and PGE2 falls, the set point drops to 37 °C while the body is still at 39 °C, so the hypothalamus reads overheating: the skin flushes and the patient sweats. In heat stroke, by contrast, the set point is normal and heat gain exceeds heat loss, so COX inhibition does not lower the temperature.
Predicting lesions of the feeding centers

Leptin rises with fat mass and acts on the arcuate nucleus, stimulating POMC neurons (whose product alpha-MSH acts on melanocortin-4 receptors to cause satiety) and inhibiting NPY and AgRP neurons, which promote hunger. Ghrelin from the empty stomach does the reverse. Destroying the ventromedial satiety region leaves hunger unopposed, so the animal or patient overeats and becomes obese. Destroying the lateral area removes the drive to eat, causing anorexia and wasting even with food available. Loss-of-function mutations in leptin, its receptor, or MC4R cause severe early obesity by the same logic.

blocks.predict: What would happen to temperature and feeding after a tumor destroyed the ventromedial nucleus but spared the anterior hypothalamus?
blocks.explain: Hunger from the lateral area would be unopposed, giving hyperphagia and obesity, while heat loss responses would remain intact.

sections.title: The limbic system, memory, and emotion

blocks.text: The limbic system is a ring of cortical and subcortical structures on the medial edge of the cerebral hemisphere that links memory, emotion, and the hypothalamus. Its core parts are the hippocampus and amygdala in the medial temporal lobe, the parahippocampal and cingulate gyri, the fornix, the mammillary bodies of the hypothalamus, and the anterior nucleus of the thalamus. Through the hypothalamus, limbic activity produces the autonomic and endocrine signs of emotion, such as a racing heart with fear.

blocks.title: The Papez circuit
blocks.caption: Damage anywhere in this loop, especially bilaterally, can impair formation of new declarative memories.

blocks.text: The hippocampus binds the elements of an experience into a declarative (explicit) memory trace, using NMDA receptor dependent long-term potentiation. Over months to years the trace is consolidated into neocortex and no longer needs the hippocampus. Bilateral hippocampal damage therefore causes anterograde amnesia: new facts and events cannot be stored, while older memories, language, intelligence, and procedural (skill) learning are spared. Retrograde loss, if present, is temporally graded, affecting the most recent memories that were not yet consolidated. Causes include global hypoxia (CA1 pyramidal neurons are especially vulnerable), HSV-1 encephalitis, bilateral posterior cerebral artery infarcts, and Alzheimer disease, which begins in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus.
Thiamine deficiency and the diencephalic memory relays

Thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase, and transketolase. In deficiency, usually with chronic alcohol use and poor intake, neurons with high oxidative demand fail to make ATP, lactate accumulates, and symmetric lesions with petechial hemorrhage form around the third ventricle, aqueduct, and fourth ventricle: mammillary bodies, medial dorsal thalamus, periaqueductal gray, ocular motor and vestibular nuclei, and the cerebellar vermis. A carbohydrate load increases flux through these enzymes and can unmask or worsen deficiency.

Wernicke encephalopathy is the acute stage: confusion, eye signs (nystagmus and ophthalmoplegia, classically lateral rectus weakness), and gait ataxia, each traceable to the structures above, though all three appear together in a minority of patients. Korsakoff syndrome is the chronic stage, with severe anterograde and some retrograde amnesia and confabulation; it reflects damage to the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus, which interrupts the Papez circuit and related thalamic pathways. Atrophic mammillary bodies are a characteristic imaging and autopsy finding.
The amygdala and Klüver-Bucy syndrome

The amygdala, deep in the anterior temporal lobe in front of the hippocampus, assigns emotional value to sensory input, especially fear, and drives fear responses through its central nucleus projections to the hypothalamus and brainstem. Bilateral destruction of the anterior temporal lobes including the amygdala, classically from HSV-1 encephalitis, trauma, or frontotemporal degeneration, produces Klüver-Bucy syndrome: hyperorality (placing objects in the mouth), hypersexuality and disinhibition, placidity with loss of fear, visual agnosia, and hypermetamorphosis (compulsive attention to every visual stimulus).

Anterograde amnesia; skills and old memories spared
Wernicke triad acutely; Korsakoff amnesia with confabulation
Apathy, reduced motivation; akinetic mutism if bilateral

blocks.predict: Why does a patient with bilateral hippocampal infarcts still remember childhood events and can learn to ride a stationary bike?
blocks.explain: Old memories are already consolidated in neocortex, and procedural learning uses the basal ganglia and cerebellum, not the hippocampus.

blocks.text: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) contains neurons that keep time on their own. In each cell, the CLOCK and BMAL1 proteins activate transcription of the Period and Cryptochrome genes, whose proteins accumulate and then inhibit CLOCK and BMAL1. This transcription and translation feedback loop takes slightly more or less than 24 hours, so the clock must be reset daily. Light provides the reset: intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells containing melanopsin, most sensitive to blue light, project through the retinohypothalamic tract to the SCN, independent of the visual pathway to the lateral geniculate body.

blocks.title: From light to melatonin
steps: Descending fibers reach upper thoracic intermediolateral column
Superior cervical ganglion sends sympathetic fibers to pineal
Norepinephrine on beta-1 receptors raises pinealocyte cAMP
Melatonin secreted into blood at night
blocks.caption: Light at night reverses the chain and suppresses melatonin within minutes.

blocks.text: Melatonin is synthesized from tryptophan, which tryptophan hydroxylase converts to 5-hydroxytryptophan and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase converts to serotonin. In the pineal gland, serotonin N-acetyltransferase (the rate-limiting, night-activated step) and a methyltransferase convert serotonin to melatonin. Plasma melatonin rises after dark and peaks in the middle of the night. It acts on MT1 and MT2 receptors, including receptors on the SCN itself, promoting sleep onset and shifting the clock. Because the pineal pathway runs through the cervical sympathetic chain, high spinal cord injury or interruption of that chain can abolish the melatonin rhythm, and people with no light perception may run on a clock that drifts away from the 24-hour day.
Orexin and the stability of waking

Orexin A and B (hypocretin 1 and 2) are made only by neurons in the lateral and perifornical hypothalamus. They excite the arousal systems: locus coeruleus (norepinephrine), dorsal raphe (serotonin), tuberomammillary nucleus (histamine), and cholinergic pontine and basal forebrain nuclei. These arousal systems also suppress REM-generating neurons. Orexin therefore acts like a stabilizer on the switch between waking, non-REM, and REM sleep, keeping each state consolidated.

Narcolepsy type 1 results from selective loss of orexin neurons, thought to be autoimmune because of a strong association with HLA-DQB1*06:02, and is confirmed by low CSF hypocretin-1. Without orexin, states switch abruptly. Patients have excessive daytime sleepiness and fragmented night sleep, enter REM within minutes of falling asleep, and experience REM features during waking: hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations (dream imagery at sleep onset or waking) and sleep paralysis. Cataplexy is the defining feature: strong positive emotion such as laughter triggers the brainstem REM atonia pathway, causing sudden loss of muscle tone, from jaw sagging to a full collapse, while consciousness is preserved. Narcolepsy type 2 lacks cataplexy and usually has normal hypocretin levels.

blocks.title: Worked example: localizing a sleep attack
blocks.text: A 19-year-old falls asleep in class daily and drops his coffee cup when he laughs, though he remains aware. Sleep testing shows REM within 10 minutes of sleep onset. The awareness during collapse excludes a seizure or syncope and points to REM atonia intruding into waking. Early REM shows that REM is no longer held off by monoaminergic tone. The single lesion that destabilizes both is loss of orexin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, so CSF hypocretin-1 would be low. The SCN is intact, so the timing of his sleep across the 24 hours is normal; the problem is the stability of each state, not the clock.

sections.title: REM sleep behavior disorder, N3 parasomnias, and restless legs syndrome

blocks.text: Sleep cycles about every 90 minutes through non-REM stages N1, N2 (sleep spindles and K complexes), and N3 (high-amplitude delta waves, the deepest stage), then REM sleep. N3 dominates the first third of the night, and REM periods lengthen toward morning. During REM the EEG resembles waking and the eyes move rapidly, but pontine neurons near the locus coeruleus drive medullary circuits that release glycine and GABA onto spinal and cranial motor neurons, producing REM atonia. Where a parasomnia arises in this architecture predicts its timing, recall, and behavior.
REM sleep behavior disorder

In REM sleep behavior disorder, the atonia pathway is damaged, so dream content is acted out with punching, kicking, or shouting, often injuring the patient or bed partner. Episodes occur in the second half of the night, when REM is abundant, and the patient wakes quickly and can recount a vivid, often threatening dream. Polysomnography shows REM sleep without atonia. The disorder is most common in men over 50. Alpha-synuclein deposition reaches the lower brainstem early in Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy, before the substantia nigra and cortex are heavily involved, so isolated REM sleep behavior disorder often precedes these diseases by years and most patients develop one of them on long follow-up.
N3 parasomnias of childhood

Sleepwalking, sleep terrors, and confusional arousals are disorders of partial arousal from N3. Motor and limbic regions become active while frontal and parietal association cortex stays in slow-wave sleep, so the child walks or screams with eyes open but is unresponsive, hard to wake, confused if woken, and has no memory of the event. A sleep terror adds intense autonomic arousal: tachycardia, sweating, dilated pupils. Because N3 is plentiful in children and in the first third of the night, these events are common in childhood, cluster early in the night, increase after sleep deprivation (which deepens N3) or fever, and fade as N3 declines with age. Nightmares differ: they arise in REM, later in the night, and the child wakes fully and recalls the dream.
Restless legs syndrome

Restless legs syndrome is a sensorimotor disorder, not a parasomnia, defined by an urge to move the legs, often with uncomfortable creeping sensations, that begins or worsens at rest, is worse in the evening and at night, and is relieved by movement. Most patients also have periodic limb movements during sleep. The leading mechanism is brain iron deficiency: iron is the cofactor of tyrosine hydroxylase and is needed for dopamine signaling, and imaging and CSF studies show low iron in the substantia nigra. Dopaminergic activity normally falls in the evening, which fits the timing. Secondary causes include iron deficiency (low ferritin), chronic kidney disease, and pregnancy; dopamine-blocking drugs and sedating antihistamines worsen symptoms.

integration.text: Anatomy and physiology explain the hypothalamus as a set of controllers placed at the meeting point of blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and nerve. Circumventricular organs let it read plasma osmolality and circulating cytokines, portal vessels and axonal transport carry its hormones, and descending autonomic pathways reach sweat glands, skin vessels, brown fat, and the pineal gland. Immunology and biochemistry supply the signals: IL-1 and PGE2 reset temperature, leptin and ghrelin report energy balance, thiamine pyrophosphate keeps memory relays supplied with ATP, and tryptophan feeds serotonin and melatonin.

Pathology ties lesions to signs. Suprasellar tumors, viral encephalitis, nutritional deficiency, autoimmune neuron loss, and alpha-synuclein deposition each damage a different node and produce a recognizable syndrome. The limits matter: hypothalamic centers are networks rather than discrete points, human lesions are rarely confined to one nucleus, and sleep disorders are confirmed by polysomnography and history rather than by a single test.

summary: Supraoptic and paraventricular neurons release ADH and oxytocin from the posterior pituitary; arcuate dopamine inhibits prolactin and arcuate GHRH stimulates GH.
Lateral hypothalamic lesions cause anorexia and ventromedial lesions cause hyperphagia, because each removes one of two opposed controllers; leptin acts on the arcuate nucleus to promote satiety.
The anterior hypothalamus drives heat loss and the posterior drives heat conservation, so their lesions cause hyperthermia and hypothermia or poikilothermia.
Fever is a raised set point: IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha induce COX-2 at the OVLT, and PGE2 on preoptic EP3 receptors raises the set point; hyperthermia has a normal set point.
The Papez circuit runs hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus, cingulate gyrus, and back.

Bilateral hippocampal damage causes anterograde amnesia with old memories and skills spared; thiamine deficiency damages mammillary bodies and medial thalamus, giving Wernicke encephalopathy and Korsakoff amnesia with confabulation.
Bilateral amygdala damage, often from HSV-1, causes Klüver-Bucy syndrome with hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity, and visual agnosia.
Melanopsin retinal ganglion cells reset the SCN, which controls pineal melatonin through a sympathetic relay; melatonin rises in darkness.
Loss of lateral hypothalamic orexin neurons causes narcolepsy type 1 with cataplexy, sleep-onset REM, sleep paralysis, and low CSF hypocretin.
REM sleep behavior disorder (late night, dream recall) often precedes synucleinopathy; N3 parasomnias (early night, no recall) affect children; restless legs syndrome is linked to iron deficiency.

verify: Standard textbooks agree that both supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei make ADH and oxytocin; confirm that NABNE expects the simplified pairing (supraoptic with ADH, paraventricular with oxytocin) as the keyed answer.
The registry lists GHRH under the arcuate nucleus; GnRH neurons lie in the arcuate and preoptic regions as well, and this chapter does not test GnRH.
Posterior hypothalamic lesions are given as hypothermia in review books and as poikilothermia in neuroanatomy texts; confirm which wording NABNE uses.

The proportion of isolated REM sleep behavior disorder that converts to a synucleinopathy is quoted from about 70% to over 90% depending on follow-up length; this chapter states only that most patients convert.
Ferritin thresholds used to define iron deficiency in restless legs syndrome vary (often about 50 to 75 ng/mL, higher than the general anemia cutoff); confirm whether NABNE tests a specific value.

Diagnostic cutoffs for narcolepsy (CSF hypocretin-1 at or below 110 pg/mL, mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with at least two sleep-onset REM periods) follow ICSD-3 and are not stated in the text; confirm whether they are tested.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Papez circuit and Klüver-Bucy syndrome and the term OVLT, or only descriptive terms.
